title: Reference-state dependence and interface scaling of superfluid response in a two-dimensional crystal
abstract: Grain boundaries modify both transport paths and the surrounding crystal, making their contribution to superfluid stiffness difficult to isolate. We quantify these contributions in stationary two-dimensional soft-core Gross--Pitaevskii (GP) crystals using tensor response, independently prepared bicrystals, and measured interface lengths. A one-percent change of lattice spacing alters the bulk stiffness by approximately 5--9\%, comparable to the boundary contribution. For the same defective state, two bulk references give relative excesses of 0.027\% and 4.15\%. Matching the comparator to grain strain and chemical potential yields positive diagonal excesses in paired preparations at three interaction strengths. Within a twelve-state family with comparable grain interiors, the excess is robust to 288 bulk substitutions and follows an approximate length-per-area relation. Independent fixed-area pairs yield a line-response coefficient 3.1\% higher than the three-size estimate. Size and directional dependence restrict this relation to the specified crystal conditions. Reduced link networks relate the directional response to the organization of boundary connections but do not accurately resolve every small bulk-subtracted excess. The results distinguish boundary enhancement from changes in the surrounding crystal and establish a quantitative comparison protocol for superfluid transport in defective crystals.
summary: This theoretical work investigates the superfluid stiffness in 2D soft-core Bose crystals containing grain boundaries. By using tensor response formalism, the authors develop a method to isolate the true contribution of the boundaries from bulk material variations. The findings provide a quantitative protocol for analyzing superfluid transport in defective quantum materials.
main_problem: The paper aims to quantify the contribution of grain boundaries to the superfluid stiffness in a two-dimensional crystal and determine how this contribution depends on the chosen reference state.
main_result: The authors establish a quantitative comparison protocol that successfully distinguishes boundary enhancement from changes in the surrounding crystal, recommending a strain- and chemical-potential-matched composite as the best reference state.
method: The study employs the tensor response formalism applied to a soft-core Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) crystal, comparing measured grain stiffness to bulk composites derived using various reference conventions.
model_or_system: The system is a superfluid confined in a two-dimensional soft-core Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) crystal, modeled by a nonlocal GP Hamiltonian. The analysis focuses on bicrystals containing grain boundaries.
key_observables: Superfluid stiffness tensor (f_s or K), grain boundary enhancement ($\Delta \mathbf{K}$), interface length ($\ell$), and the effective half-trace coefficient ($\Gamma_{K, 	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Lattice spacing changes (1% variation), interaction strengths, and the geometry of the grain boundaries.
main_assumptions: The superfluid stiffness is not treated as a Gibbs surface excess, and the comparison relies on matching mechanical geometry (strain) and particle-exchange conditions (chemical potential).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate density and local phase stiffness in relaxed bicrystals, showing directional excess and bulk-reference dependence across different preparation methods.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the superfluid stiffness using tensor response, quantifying the excess contribution ($\Delta \mathbf{K}$), comparing results across various bulk reference states (e.g., fixed-mass vs. $\mu$-matched), and concluding with a robust protocol for separating boundary effects.
why_interesting: The rigorous quantification of boundary effects in superfluid systems, particularly the sensitivity to reference state definitions, is crucial for accurately modeling real-world, imperfect quantum materials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Density and local phase stiffness of relaxed bicrystals. Columns show ρ on the linear scale [0, 14], ex, and ey; stiffness uses log10(ej/n0) ∈[−7, 0]. Rows 1–2 show the 30◦family at L = 128; rows 3–4 show the low-angle family at L = 256, with final misorientation 15.75◦. Dashed boxes locate the 32 × 32 zoom windows. Red circles mark non-sixfold coordination. Fields are shown without smoothing; stationary residuals are 9.99 × 10−9 and 5.93 × 10−11.

FIG. 2. Directional excess and bulk-reference dependence for thirty-two independently prepared bicrystals. Symbols show size means; error bars describe preparation resampling. Panel (a) uses the recommended strain- and chemical-potential-matched reference; both diagonal excesses are positive. Panel (b) includes that reference as a dashed black curve with open circles, nearly coincident with the native-density curve. Different bulk conventions define different excess observables.

FIG. 3. Microscopic transport and reference-controlled response. (a) Inter-peak density in grain interiors and boundary regions; the line is the empirical interior fit over its sampled range. (b) Diagonal network and GP stiffnesses at Λ = 128.68, with one calibrated coupling constant. (c) Ratio of the mean stiffness changes produced by halving equal numbers of boundary and interior couplings on each fixed network; labels give angle and box side. (d) GP excess relative to strain- and chemical-potential-matched composites for two paired preparations across interaction strengths. Connecting lines identify the same preparation branch.

FIG. 4. Preparation-specific coefficients under different bulk conventions and their association with crystalline structure. Error bars show preparation resampling; correlations are evaluated within size.

FIG. 5. Interface scaling with comparable grain interiors. (a) Individual physical excesses with proportional and quadratic fits. (b) Directional size-mean effective coefficients; error bars are resampling summaries over three to five states per size.
